s: Knowledge is a being
q: When Knowledge travelled north, across the Black Water, and over the Dark-Steep Mountain, he met Do-nothing Say-nothing and asked of him as follows:

s: Yellow Emperor is a being
q: So when Knowledge got no reply, he went back to the palace and asked the Yellow Emperor.

s: Yellow Emperor states TAO may be known by no thoughts or cogitations
q: "By no thoughts, by no cogitations, TAO may be known.

s: Yellow Emperor states TAO may be approached by resting in nothing and according in nothing
q: By resting in nothing, by according in nothing, TAO may be approached.

s: Yellow Emperor states TAO may be attained by following nothing and pursuing nothing
q: By following nothing, by pursuing nothing, TAO may be attained."

s: TAO is a principle (unnameable and formless)
q: That which imparts form to forms is itself formless; therefore TAO cannot have a name.

s: TAO is omnipresent all things (there is nowhere where it is not)
q: "There is nowhere," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "where it is not."

s: TAO is indivisible ONE (all things are one through it)
q: Therefore all things are ONE.

s: TAO cannot be attained by knowledge (attainment requires absence of knowledge)
q: TAO is attained, not by knowledge, but by absence of knowledge.

s: TAO is spontaneous spontaneity (in the operation of the perfect man)
q: Unfathomable as the sea, wondrously ending only to begin again, informing all creation without being exhausted, the TAO of the perfect man is spontaneous in its operation.

s: Knowledge asks about TAO (seeking how it may be known, approached, and attained)
q: "Kindly tell me by what thoughts, by what cogitations, may TAO be known? By resting in what, by according in what, may TAO be approached? By following what, by pursuing what, may TAO be attained?"

s: TAO causes THE UNIVERSE (without itself being a thing)
q: TAO makes things what they are, but is not itself a thing.

s: TAO is within everything (and continues to produce without end)
q: Nothing can produce TAO; yet everything has TAO within it, and continues to produce it without end.

s: TAO causes fulness
q: TAO causes fulness and emptiness, but it is not either.

s: TAO causes emptiness
q: TAO causes fulness and emptiness, but it is not either.

s: TAO causes renovation
q: It causes renovation and decay, but it is not either.

s: TAO causes decay
q: It causes renovation and decay, but it is not either.

s: TAO causes beginning
q: It causes beginning and end, but it is not either.

s: TAO causes end
q: It causes beginning and end, but it is not either.

s: TAO is not objective value (when manifested)
q: Manifested, TAO has no objective value; hence silence is better than argument.

s: Virtue is a exemplification of TAO
q: Virtue (TÊ), here the exemplification of TAO.

s: Perfect Man teaches doctrine (without expression in words)
q: Therefore the Sage teaches a doctrine which does not find expression in words.

s: Perfect Man performs nothing (beyond gazing at the universe)
q: Hence the saying that the perfect man does nothing, the true Sage performs nothing, beyond gazing at the universe.

s: Perfect Man venerates ONE (because all things are permeated by one vital fluid)
q: The world is permeated by a single vital fluid, and Sages accordingly venerate ONE."

s: Perfect Man adapts to external world (without violating or clinging to social relations)
q: The true Sage who meets with these, does not violate them. Neither does he continue to hold fast by them.

s: Perfect Man finds salvation in diminution (without loss)
q: It is in addition without gain, in diminution without loss, that the true Sage finds salvation.

s: universe is beautiful beauty (and says nothing)
q: The universe is very beautiful, yet it says nothing.

s: universe contains four seasons (which abide by a fixed law)
q: The four seasons abide by a fixed law, yet they are not heard.

s: universe is based on absolute principles (without speaking)
q: All creation is based upon absolute principles, yet nothing speaks.

s: God delegates body (as image)
q: "It is the delegated image of God," replied Ch'êng.

s: Do-nothing Say-nothing is a being
q: he met Do-nothing Say-nothing and asked of him as follows:

s: God delegates life (as harmony)
q: Your life is not your own. It is the delegated harmony of God.

s: God delegates individuality (as adaptability)
q: Your individuality is not your own. It is the delegated adaptability of God.

s: God delegates posterity (as exuviæ)
q: Your posterity is not your own. It is the delegated exuviæ of God.

s: THE UNIVERSE contains TAO (in every thing, including the smallest)
q: An autumn spikelet, in all its minuteness, must carry TAO within itself.

s: THE UNIVERSE is informed by TAO (without exhaustion)
q: the TAO of the perfect man is spontaneous in its operation. That all creation can be informed by it without exhaustion, is its TAO.

s: vital fluid produces life (through convergence)
q: The life of man results from convergence of the vital fluid. Its convergence is life; its dispersion, death.

s: vital fluid produces death (through dispersion)
q: The life of man results from convergence of the vital fluid. Its convergence is life; its dispersion, death.

s: Confucius states TAO existed before the universe
q: What there was before the universe, was TAO.

s: Do-nothing Say-nothing knows TAO (genuinely, through not knowing)
q: "Of those two," replied the Yellow Emperor, "Do-nothing Say-nothing is genuinely right

s: Confucius states there is no past, present, beginning, or end
q: There is no past, no present, no beginning, no end.

s: Confucius teaches natural intelligence (clarity comes from direct appeal to it)
q: Your clearness of yesterday," answered Confucius, "was because my answer appealed direct to your natural intelligence.

s: Do-nothing Say-nothing does not answer Knowledge (because he could not answer)
q: To these three questions, Do-nothing Say-nothing returned no answer. Not that he would not answer, but that he could not.

s: All-in-extremes is a being
q: where he saw All-in-extremes, and to him he put the same questions.

s: All-in-extremes knows TAO (nearly, through forgetting what he would say)
q: "Of those two," replied the Yellow Emperor, "Do-nothing Say-nothing is genuinely right, and All-in-extremes is near.

s: All-in-extremes forgets what he wanted to say (just as he was about to speak)
q: But just as he was about to speak he forgot what he wanted to say.

s: Kêng Sang Ch'u is a disciple of Lao Tzŭ
q: Among the disciples of Lao Tzŭ was one named Kêng Sang Ch'u.

s: Lao Tzŭ is master of Kêng Sang Ch'u
q: He alone had attained to the TAO of his Master.

s: Lao Tzŭ recognizes Nan Yung Ch'u (as coming from Kêng Sang Ch'u)
q: "Have you come from Kêng Sang Ch'u?" said the latter.

s: Lao Tzŭ diagnoses Nan Yung Ch'u (as confused and estranged from his natural self)
q: You are confused, as a child that has lost its parents. You would fathom the sea with a pole. You are astray. You are struggling to get back to your natural self, but cannot find the way.

s: Lao Tzŭ teaches art of preserving life (as keeping all in one and avoiding care)
q: The art of preserving life," replied Lao Tzŭ, "consists in being able to keep all in ONE, _Sc._ Body and soul.

s: Nan Yung Ch'u is a disciple
q: Nan Yung Ch'u A disciple.

s: Nan Yung Ch'u seeks TAO (while troubled by moral dilemmas)
q: My trouble lies in not seeing how to escape from these three dilemmas. On the strength of my connection with Kêng Sang, I would venture to ask advice.

s: Nan Yung Ch'u hears TAO (only with his ears at first)
q: But so far I only hear TAO with my ears.

s: Nan Yung Ch'u cultivates good (within himself)
q: Nan Yung begged to be allowed to remain, and set to work to cultivate the good and eliminate the evil within him.

s: Nan Yung Ch'u eliminates evil (within himself)
q: Nan Yung begged to be allowed to remain, and set to work to cultivate the good and eliminate the evil within him.

s: TAO is a Portal of God (through which all pass in and out without seeing its form)
q: That through which one passes in and out without seeing its form, that is the Portal of God.

s: Kêng Sang Ch'u attained TAO (alone among Lao Tzŭ's disciples)
q: He alone had attained to the TAO of his Master.

s: TAO informs existence (through its subdivisions, successes and failures)
q: TAO informs its own subdivisions, their successes and their failures.

s: TAO is unconditioned (when the mind reaches repose and clear perception)
q: And being unconditioned, it will be in that state of inaction by which there is nothing which cannot be accomplished.

s: TAO is sovereign lord (of TÊ)
q: TAO is the sovereign lord of TÊ.

s: TAO proceeds from the real self (from God)
q: All "virtue" should proceed from the real self, _sc._ from God.

s: perfect man shares food of this earth (while sharing the happiness of God)
q: The perfect man shares the food of this earth, but the happiness of God.

s: perfect man is free from care (and unconscious in action)
q: Free from care he comes, and unconscious he goes;--this is the art of preserving life.

s: perfect man does not incur trouble from men
q: He does not incur trouble either from men or things.

s: Sages of old resides in Nothing (as the abiding-place of the Sage)
q: The Portal of God is Non-Existence. All things sprang from Non-Existence. Existence could not make existence existence. It must have proceeded from Non-Existence, The idea of existence, independent of its correlate, cannot be apprehended by the human intellect. And Non-Existence and Nothing are ONE. If all things sprang from non-existence, it might be urged that non-existence had an objective existence. But non-existence is nothing, and nothing excludes the idea of something, making subjective and objective nothings ONE. Herein is the abiding-place of the Sage.

s: Sages of old devotes itself to natural (and neglects the artificial)
q: The Sage devotes himself to the natural and neglects the artificial.

s: God assists constant people (those sought after by men)
q: Those who are constant are sought after by men and assisted by God.

s: Kêng Sang Ch'u lives on Wei-lei Mountains (up north)
q: He lived up north, on the Wei-lei Mountains.

s: God punishes people who do evil in secret (as avenging emissaries of the Deity)
q: Those who do evil in the open light of day,--men will punish them. Those who do evil in secret,--God will punish them.

s: God destroys people who do not follow perfection
q: Let knowledge stop at the unknowable. That is perfection. And for those who do not follow this, God will destroy them!

s: Nature is a bandit (the most powerful bandit)
q: There is no bandit so powerful as Nature.

s: Nature is substance of life
q: Nature is the substance of life.

s: Nature produces visible universe (through interaction of the Positive and Negative principles)
q: There is no bandit so powerful as Nature. The interaction of the Positive and Negative principles, which produces the visible universe.

s: TÊ is a Virtue (of spontaneity)
q: TAO is the sovereign lord of TÊ. TÊ is the "virtue" of spontaneity.

s: TÊ is glorified by Life
q: Life is the glorifier of TÊ.

s: Nothing produces all things (as their origin)
q: The Portal of God is Non-Existence. All things sprang from Non-Existence.

s: Nothing is one with Nothing
q: And Non-Existence and Nothing are ONE.

s: Portal of God is a Portal (of God)
q: That through which one passes in and out without seeing its form, that is the Portal of God.

s: Kêng Sang Ch'u dismissed attendants of Kêng Sang Ch'u (those who were systematically clever or conventionally charitable)
q: Of his attendants, he dismissed those who were systematically clever or conventionally charitable.

s: Portal of God is Nothing (the portal's nature)
q: The Portal of God is Non-Existence.

s: Virtue proceeds from God (when genuine)
q: All "virtue" should proceed from the real self, _sc._ from God.

s: spontaneity is a Virtue (the basis of virtue passive and virtue active)
q: Emotion which is spontaneous is called virtue passive. Emotion which is not evoked by the external is called virtue active.

s: art of preserving life consists in inaction (by which there is nothing that cannot be accomplished)
q: And being unconditioned, it will be in that state of inaction by which there is nothing which cannot be accomplished.

s: subjective point of view originates with life (with knowledge as its tutor)
q: It originates with life, and, with knowledge as its tutor, drifts into the admission of right and wrong.

s: subjective point of view treats right and wrong (as determined by one's own standard)
q: But one's own standard of right is _the_ standard, and others have to adapt themselves to it.

s: existence proceeds from Nothing (because existence cannot make itself exist)
q: Existence could not make existence existence. It must have proceeded from Non-Existence,

s: existence has great Space (as existence without limitation)
q: Existence without limitation is _Space_.

s: great Space is existence without limitation
q: Existence without limitation is _Space_.

s: Time is continuity without a starting-point
q: Continuity without a starting-point is _Time_.

s: Kêng Sang Ch'u retained attendants of Kêng Sang Ch'u (the useless and incompetent)
q: The useless remained with him; the incompetent served him.

s: Man is soot on a kettle (in the brevity and concentration of life)
q: Man's life is as the soot on a kettle.

s: Man is subject to Nature (with no escape from its operation)
q: In the whole universe there is no escape from it. Yet it is not Nature which does the injury. It is man's own heart.

s: Man causes injury (through his own heart rather than through Nature)
q: Yet it is not Nature which does the injury. It is man's own heart.

s: Kêng Sang Ch'u benefited district of Wei-lei (through his influence)
q: And in three years the district of Wei-lei was greatly benefited.

s: Kêng Sang Ch'u is honoured as a tutelary god of the land
q: Surely he must be a true Sage. Why not pray to him as to the spirits, and honour him as a tutelary god of the land?

s: Kêng Sang Ch'u feels shame before Lao Tzŭ (when people seek to exalt him)
q: On hearing of this, Kêng Sang Ch'u turned his face to the south Towards the abode of Lao Tzŭ. in shame

s: Hsü Wu Kuei is a hermit
q: Hsü Wu Kuei, introduced by Nü Shang, went to see Wu Hou of Wei. A hermit, a minister, and a prince, respectively.

s: horses are outstripped by horses of the Empire
q: They are not equal to the horses of the Empire.

s: horses move as though they had parted with their own individuality (horses of the Empire)
q: The horses of the Empire are splendid. They move as though anxious to get along, as though they had lost the way, as though they had parted with their own individuality.

s: Perfect Man is heard by Wu Hou of Wei (after a long absence)
q: Long it is, I ween, since his Highness has heard the voice of a pure man at his side!

s: Wu Hou of Wei oppresses the people (to satisfy his sensualities)
q: Your Highness is the ruler of a large State, and you oppress the whole population thereof in order to satisfy your sensualities.

s: love for the people is the root of all evil to the people
q: Love for the people is the root of all evil to the people.

s: duty to one's neighbour causes war (when cultivated to put an end to war)
q: Cultivation of duty towards one's neighbour in order to put an end to war is the origin of all fighting.

s: war originates in duty to one's neighbour (when cultivated to put an end to war)
q: Cultivation of duty towards one's neighbour in order to put an end to war is the origin of all fighting.

s: Yellow Emperor visits TAO (upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain)
q: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear.

s: Yellow Emperor has charioteer Fang Ming
q: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear.

s: Hsü Wu Kuei visits Wu Hou of Wei (introduced by Nü Shang)
q: Hsü Wu Kuei, introduced by Nü Shang, went to see Wu Hou of Wei.

s: Yellow Emperor has attendant Ch'ang Yü (seated on his right)
q: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear.

s: Yellow Emperor has outrider Chang Jo
q: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear.

s: Yellow Emperor has outrider Hsi P'êng
q: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear.

s: Yellow Emperor has rear guard K'un Hun
q: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear.

s: Yellow Emperor has rear guard Hua Chi
q: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear.

s: boy is a horse herder
q: By and by, they fell in with a boy who was grazing horses, and asked him, saying, "Do you know the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain?"

s: boy knows TAO (knows where TAO abides)
q: "And can you tell us," continued the Sages, "where TAO abides?" "I can," replied the boy.

s: boy governs the Empire (by looking after horses)
q: "I should govern the empire," said the boy, "just the same as I look after my horses. What else should I do?

s: horses' natural care requires no harm comes to the horses
q: The boy declined to answer, but on being again urged, cried out, "What difference is there between governing the empire and looking after horses? See that no harm comes to the horses, that is all!"

s: Nü Shang introduces Hsü Wu Kuei
q: Hsü Wu Kuei, introduced by Nü Shang, went to see Wu Hou of Wei.

s: the Empire is governed as horses (just the same as I look after my horses)
q: "I should govern the empire," said the boy, "just the same as I look after my horses. What else should I do?

s: Confucianists are one of five schools (discussing standards of right with Mihists, Yang Chu, Ping, and Hui Tzŭ)
q: Now there are the Confucianists, the Mihists, the schools of Yang Yang Chu. See ch. viii. and Ping, Kung Sun Lung. See ch. xvii. making with your own five in all.

s: Mihists are one of five schools (discussing standards of right with Confucianists, Yang Chu, Ping, and Hui Tzŭ)
q: Now there are the Confucianists, the Mihists, the schools of Yang Yang Chu. See ch. viii. and Ping, Kung Sun Lung. See ch. xvii. making with your own five in all.

s: Hui Tzŭ debates Confucianists (about standards of right)
q: The Confucianists, the Mihists, and the followers of Yang and Ping," replied Hui Tzŭ, "are just now engaged in discussing this matter with me.

s: Hui Tzŭ debates Mihists (about standards of right)
q: The Confucianists, the Mihists, and the followers of Yang and Ping," replied Hui Tzŭ, "are just now engaged in discussing this matter with me.

s: Hui Tzŭ is a man without sufficient TAO (according to Chuang Tzŭ's allegory)
q: A maimed man (Hui Tzŭ) should avoid quarrels. His own share of TAO is insufficient even for himself.

s: Chuang Tzŭ has no material for speech (since Hui Tzŭ perished)
q: And I too, ever since he perished, have been without my material, having no one with whom I can speak.

s: Wu Hou of Wei is a prince
q: A hermit, a minister, and a prince, respectively.

s: Ch'i State sends son (to the Sung State as a door-keeper)
q: A man of the Ch'i State," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "sent away his son into the Sung State, to be a door-keeper, with maimed body.

s: government requires natural care (according to the boy's teaching)
q: "What difference is there between governing the empire and looking after horses? See that no harm comes to the horses, that is all!"

s: moral standards are not general (when each man has his own)
q: "If there was no general standard of right in the world," continued Chuang Tzŭ, "but each man had his own, then everybody would be a Yao.

s: the people escape death (when the ruler abstains from aggression)
q: If your Highness will only abstain, that will be enough. Cultivate the sincerity that is within your breast, so as to be responsive to the conditions of your environment, and be not aggressive. The people will thus escape death;

s: passion is given TÊ (when your Highness gives free play to passion)
q: If your Highness gives free play to passion and yields to loves and hates, then the natural conditions of your existence will suffer.

s: horses have attributes straightness, curve, squareness, and roundness (horses of the State)
q: Their straightness In running. must be that of a line. Their curve must be that of an arc. Their squareness, that of the square. Their roundness, that of the compasses. One commentator applies all this to the shape of the animals.

s: horses are horses of the State
q: These are the horses of the State.

s: Kuan Chung is at point of death dying
q: Kuan Chung being at the point of death, Duke Huan went to see him.

s: Virtue is shared as true wisdom (when shared with others)
q: To share one's virtue with others is called true wisdom.

s: Virtue is multiform varied manifestations
q: With undivided TAO, TÊ cannot be coincident. The latter is multiform.

s: Prince of Wu visits Monkey Mountain (by boat)
q: The prince of Wu took a boat and went to the Monkey Mountain, which he ascended.

s: monkeys flee from Prince of Wu (in terror)
q: When the monkeys saw him, they fled in terror and hid themselves in the thicket.

s: monkeys are vulnerable to arrows (when confronted by many attackers)
q: The skill of the poor monkey availed nothing against the cloud of arrows discharged by the guards.

s: Yen Pu I receives tuition from Tung Wu (to remove superiority)
q: Yen Pu I went home, and put himself under the tuition of Tung Wu,

s: Tung Wu is a professor of TAO
q: A professor of TAO.

s: Yen Pu I avoids gaining reputation (after receiving tuition from Tung Wu)
q: He put aside all that gave him pleasure and avoided gaining reputation.

s: Duke Huan consults Kuan Chung (about administration of the State)
q: "You are ill, venerable Sir," said the Duke, "really ill. You had better say to whom, in the event of your getting worse, I am to entrust the administration of the State."

s: Tzŭ Ch'i of Nan-poh is a spiritual practitioner (seeking absorption into TAO)
q: And become like dry wood, my soul absorbed into TAO.

s: Tzŭ Ch'i of Nan-poh is recognized by T'ien Ho (as a Sage)
q: Now I must have given some indication by which he recognised me. As a Sage.

s: reputation displaces reality (as reputation comes)
q: As reputation comes, reality goes.

s: Confucius is entertained at banquet (by the prince of Ch'u)
q: When Confucius went to Ch'u, the prince entertained him at a banquet.

s: Ch'u State hosts Confucius (at a banquet)
q: When Confucius went to Ch'u, the prince entertained him at a banquet.

s: Sun Shu Ao is associated with goblet (at the banquet)
q: Sun Shu Ao stood up with a goblet of wine in his hand,

s: I Liao of Shih-nan is associated with libation (at the banquet)
q: and I Liao of Shih-nan poured a libation, saying, "On such occasions as this, the men of old were wont to make some utterance."

s: I Liao of Shih-nan belongs to Shih-nan
q: and I Liao of Shih-nan poured a libation, saying, "On such occasions as this, the men of old were wont to make some utterance."

s: wordless utterances is a doctrine (Confucius's doctrine)
q: "Mine," replied Confucius, "is the doctrine of wordless utterances.

s: wordless utterances is an argument of silence
q: His was the argument of silence.

s: Pao Yü is a pure and incorruptible man
q: "He is pure, incorruptible, and good.

s: Inaction achieves political results (through the TAO of inaction)
q: "Theirs was the TAO of inaction. His was the argument of silence.

s: universe is great immeasurably (because it rejects nothing)
q: The sea does not reject the streams which flow eastward into it. Therefore it is immeasurably great.

s: Sages of old benefits the people (throughout the empire without respect to persons)
q: The true Sage folds the universe in his bosom. His good influence benefits all throughout the empire, without respect to persons.

s: Sages of old does not take credit for realities (attributes them to circumstances)
q: He does not take credit for realities. But attributes it all to circumstances.

s: greatness and smallness is not secured by talking well
q: A man is not considered a good man because he is a good talker. How much less in the case of greatness?

s: Chiu Fang Yin is a physiognomist
q: Tzŭ Chi had eight sons. He ranged them before him, and summoning Chiu Fang Yin, said to him, "Examine my sons physiognomically, and tell me which will be the fortunate one."

s: K'un is a fortunate son (according to Chiu Fang Yin's physiognomy)
q: "K'un," replied Chiu Fang Yin, "will be the fortunate one."

s: K'un eats at table of a prince (as the basis of his supposed fortune)
q: "K'un," said Chiu Fang Yin, "will eat at the table of a prince, and so end his days."

s: Tzŭ Chi's sons roam through universe (with their father)
q: My sons and I do but roam through the universe.

s: Pao Yü does not associate with people unlike himself
q: With those who are not like himself, he will not associate.

s: K'un's capture by brigands results in loss of feet (before sale into Ch'i State)
q: So they cut off his feet and sold him into the Ch'i State, where he became door-keeper to Duke Chü and had meat to his dinner for the rest of his life.

s: brigands capture K'un's capture by brigands (to sell him)
q: Shortly afterwards, when K'un was on his way to the Yen State, he was captured by brigands.

s: K'un becomes door-keeper (to Duke Chü in the Ch'i State)
q: So they cut off his feet and sold him into the Ch'i State, where he became door-keeper to Duke Chü and had meat to his dinner for the rest of his life.

s: Yeh Ch'üeh questions Hsü Yu (about his destination)
q: Yeh Ch'üeh meeting Hsü Yu, said to him, "Where are you going?"

s: Hsü Yu avoids Yao (because of Yao's charity)
q: "Away from Yao!" replied the latter.

s: Yao is devoted to charity (to the exclusion of other concerns)
q: "Yao," said Hsü Yu, "thinks of nothing but charity.

s: charity attracts the people (when expressed as love)
q: There is no difficulty in winning the people. Love them and they will draw near.

s: duty to one's neighbour is not disinterested self-interest (when used as a virtue)
q: For the operation of these virtues is not disinterested.

s: Pao Yü does not forget men's wrong-doing (once heard)
q: And if he has once heard of a man's wrong-doing, he never forgets it.

s: Shun is an example of enthusiasts
q: Of enthusiasts, Shun is an example.

s: Shun attracts the people (because of a frowsy quality)
q: Mutton has a frowsy smell; and there is a frowsiness about Shun which attracts the people.

s: Shun is appointed to barren region (by Yao)
q: Then Yao, hearing of his goodness, appointed him to a barren region, trusting, as he said, that Shun's arrival would enrich it.

s: Divine man dislikes crowd (because diversity prevents advantage from accruing)
q: So it is that the spiritual man dislikes a crowd.

s: Divine man trusts natural development of events (without introducing the artificial)
q: Therefore, the divine man trusts to the natural development of events. He does not strive to introduce the artificial into the domain of the natural.

s: Pao Yü causes conflict with Duke Huan (if employed in administration of the empire)
